-- =====================================================================
-- Admin metric views. Computed in SQL so the UI just reads them. Money in
-- cents. Read server-side via the service-role client behind an admin route
-- guard; access is revoked from anon/authenticated so non-admins can't query
-- the aggregates directly.
-- =====================================================================

create view public.admin_metrics_strategic as
select
  coalesce((select sum(total_price_cents) from public.sessions where status = 'completed'), 0)::bigint as gmv_cents,
  coalesce((select sum(commission_cents) from public.sessions where status = 'completed'), 0)::bigint as revenue_cents,
  coalesce((select sum(provider_earnings_cents) from public.sessions where status = 'completed'), 0)::bigint as provider_earnings_cents,
  (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'approved')::int as active_providers,
  (select count(distinct customer_id) from public.bookings)::int as active_customers,
  coalesce((select round(avg(rating)::numeric, 2) from public.reviews), 0)::numeric as avg_rating;

create view public.admin_metrics_operational as
select
  (select count(*) from public.bookings)::int as total_bookings,
  (select count(*) from public.sessions where status = 'completed')::int as completed_sessions,
  case
    when (select count(*) from public.bookings) > 0
      then round(
        (select count(*) from public.sessions where status = 'completed')::numeric
        / (select count(*) from public.bookings) * 100, 1)
    else 0
  end as booking_to_session_pct,
  (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'approved')::int as approved_providers,
  (select count(distinct provider_id) from public.sessions where status = 'completed')::int as activated_providers,
  case
    when (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'approved') > 0
      then round(
        (select count(distinct provider_id) from public.sessions where status = 'completed')::numeric
        / (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'approved') * 100, 1)
    else 0
  end as provider_activation_pct,
  (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'approved' and is_available_now)::int as available_now,
  (select count(*) from public.bookings where status in ('confirmed', 'in_progress'))::int as open_requests;

create view public.admin_metrics_alerts as
select
  (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'pending')::int as approval_backlog,
  (select count(*) from public.reports where status = 'open')::int as open_reports,
  (select count(*) from public.providers where status = 'suspended')::int as suspended_providers,
  (select count(*) from public.bookings where status = 'cancelled')::int as cancelled_bookings,
  case
    when (select count(*) from public.bookings) > 0
      then round(
        (select count(*) from public.bookings where status = 'cancelled')::numeric
        / (select count(*) from public.bookings) * 100, 1)
    else 0
  end as cancellation_pct,
  (select count(*) from public.payments where status = 'failed')::int as failed_payments;

revoke all on public.admin_metrics_strategic from anon, authenticated;
revoke all on public.admin_metrics_operational from anon, authenticated;
revoke all on public.admin_metrics_alerts from anon, authenticated;

findings.title: Reinstating a provider unconditionally sets provider status to 'approved', bypassing the approval/background-check gate
findings.detail:
`setUserSuspended` flips provider status with `status: suspended ? "suspended" : "approved"`. The provider_status enum has four values: 'pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'suspended'. The action treats suspension as a simple approved⇄suspended toggle, but the target provider may currently be 'pending' or 'rejected'. Two concrete defects introduced by this diff:
1. Suspending a 'pending' or 'rejected' provider overwrites their real status with 'suspended', destroying the original state (no record of what it was).
2. Reinstating then sets status to 'approved' regardless of the pre-suspension state — silently auto-approving a provider who was never approved (e.g. one who hasn't cleared the background check, or was explicitly 'rejected'). This bypasses the M3 approval gate and is safety-relevant for a marketplace whose providers are vetted.
This is fully reachable from the UI: components/admin/UsersTable.tsx renders a Suspend button for every non-admin row (including pending/rejected providers), and components/admin/ReportCard.tsx's 'Suspend target' calls the same action.
findings.suggestion: Don't infer the reinstated status. Read the provider's status before suspending and, on suspend, only move 'approved' providers to 'suspended' (leave 'pending'/'rejected' as-is, or store the prior status). On reinstate, restore the saved prior status (or only un-suspend providers whose current status is 'suspended', mapping back to 'approved' only when they were approved before). Alternatively, gate the provider-status write on `target` provider status === 'approved'/'suspended' so pending/rejected providers are never auto-approved.

findings.title: Admin user search interpolates raw input into a PostgREST .or() filter string (latent injection / breaks on special chars)
findings.detail: `listUsers` builds `term = "%" + search.trim() + "%"` and interpolates it directly into `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)`. PostgREST parses the .or() argument as a filter grammar where ',' separates conditions and '(' ')' group them. Unescaped user input therefore (a) breaks legitimate searches — searching a name containing a comma or parentheses (e.g. "Smith, John" or "(work)") splits/garbles the filter or 400s, and (b) is a latent filter-injection pattern (an attacker-controlled value can append extra OR conditions like `,role.eq.admin`). The security blast radius is limited because the call is behind requireRole("admin") and targets profiles, which admins can already read in full via RLS — so there is no privilege escalation or data exposure beyond what the admin already has. Severity is low for that reason, but the correctness bug on normal inputs is real and this is the only .or() string in the codebase.
findings.suggestion: Avoid embedding raw input in the .or() filter string. Either escape PostgREST-reserved characters (wrap the value in double quotes for like/ilike and strip/escape internal quotes), or replace the single .or() with a safer construction (e.g. two separate ilike queries unioned in JS, or quote the pattern: `full_name.ilike."${escaped}"`). At minimum sanitize commas/parentheses/asterisks before interpolation.
